notes.abiri: “Two tens”. Numbers that count things agree with them: ebitabo ikumi na bibiri.
notes.mmeka: Agrees with what you count: esente zingahi, abantu bangahi.

guidebook.intro: Prices in Uganda run into thousands of shillings, so you’ll count big quickly. Numbers are built from tens, hundreds and thousands, and they agree with what you count.

tips.title: Building numbers
body: Tens are counted as “two tens”, “three tens”: **makumi abiri** (20), **makumi ashatu** (30). Add units with **na**: **ikumi na ibiri** (12). From 60 the tens have their own names: **nkaaga, nshanju, kinaana, kyenda**.
**Igana** is 100 and **magana** its plural: **magana ataano** (500). **Rukumi** is 1,000, **enkumi ibiri** 2,000, and **omutwaro** 10,000.

tips.title: Zingahi? Haggling politely
body: **Zingahi?** (how many?) agrees with esente: **Esente zingahi?** **Eki ni esente zingahi?** is “how much is this?”.
If it’s **nikiguma** (expensive), ask **Kyendeezeho** (lower it a little). When you agree: **Kare, ninkitwara** (okay, I’ll take it).

culture.title: Shillings
body: Ugandan prices are in shillings, and coins and small notes run from 100 to 1,000. Market sellers expect a little bargaining, done with a smile and a greeting first.
